unique population-based dataset. Its value is dependent on accuracy of
DBMD case classification. The MDSTARnet case definitions and the review
appronch allow a high degree of confidence in the results. It is of interest
that approximately 25% of patients lack diagnostic genetic information.

PO5.112
Diagnostic Delay in Duchenne and Becker
Muscular Dystrophy (DBMD): Data from the
MDSTARnet Cohort Emma Ciafaloni, Shree Pandya, Roch-
ester, NY, Deborah Fox, Troy, NY, Dennis Matthews, Denver, CO,
Katherine Mathews, Iowa City, IA, Timothy Miller, Tucson, AZ
OBJECTIVE: To describe the diagnostic delay in Duchenne and Becker
muscular dystrophy (DBMD) using data from a large population-based
surveillance cohort. BACKGROUND: Delayed diagnosis in DBMD has
been reported since the 1980s but it is uncertain whether such delay still
persists. Early diagnosis is crucial for timely genetic counseling and clinical
management. DESIGN/METHODS: The Muscular Dystrophy Surveil-
lance Tracking and Research Network (MD STARnet) is a surveillance
system funded by the Centers for Disease Control to identify all cases of
DBMD born since 1982 and/or residing within Arizona, Colorado, Iowa and
Western New York State. A pooled database containing clinical information
abstracted from medical records on 388 individuals was analyzed with SAS
software using non-parametric approaches to investigate the age at first
concern, time to first serum CK test and definite diagnosis in boys with and
without family history (FH) of DBMD. RESULTS: Complete data for all
variables was available for 270 boys, 81 with and 189 without FH. Median
age of first concern was 1.6 years (range 0—7.9 years) for those with FH and
4.5 years (range 0-14.6 years) for those without FH (p<.0001). Time be-
tween first concern and first CK was 3.4 months (range 0-18 months) and
10 months (range 0-48 months) for those with and without FH (p<.005).
Time between first concern and definite diagnosis was 7.4 months (range
0-24 months) and 13.5 months (range 0-48 months) for those with and
without FH (p<.0001). CONCLUSIONS/RELEVANCE: Our findings sug-
gest that diagnostic delay in DBMD still exists. Until newborn screening is
available for DBMD, steps should be taken to educate pediatricians and
primary care providers on the common DBMD presentations, the impor-

tance of early CK testing and the diagnostic strategies for boys presenting
with problems of motor function.
Supported by: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

P05.113
Utility of Needle Muscle Biopsy to Diagnosis
Inclusion Body Myositis Kirsten L. Gruis, James Teener,
Mila Blaivas, Ann Arbor, MI
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the use of percutaneous needle muscle biopsy
(NMB) in the diagnosis of inclusion body myositis (IBM). BACKGROUND:
Inclusion body myositis (IBM) is a common cause of muscle weakness in
adults and can mimic motor neuron disease and other types of myositis. A
rapid and reliable muscle biopsy technique is needed to diagnosis IBM.
Many experts contend that only the open muscle biopsy technique should
be performed. However, percutaneous NMB technique has the advantage of
a less invasive and less time consuming procedure given the lack of require-
ment for sutures and muscle clamps. DESIGN/METHODS: Muscle biopsy
data collected during routine clinical evaluation of patients with limb weak-
ness and spontaneous activity in greater than one limb by electromyogra-
phy (EMG), but without sensory impairment or upper motor neuron
dysfunction, were retrospectively analyzed. NMB with applied suction
through the University College Hospital (UCH, 5 millimeter diameter)
biopsy instrument was performed of the vastus lateralis or proximal arm
muscle. Muscle cores were gently rotated with forceps into one collective
sphere (~40-50 mg). Muscle fiber orientation using a dissection microscope
was not performed prior to pathology processing. RESULTS: Thirty pa-
tients were identified. Median age was 67 years; 50% were men. Median
symptom duration was 2 years. NMB provided a diagnosis in 26 (87%)
patients who presented with motor weakness. In combination with clinical
and electrodiagnostic findings, NMB resulted in the diagnosis of IBM in 9
igi motor neuron disease in 7 patients, inflammatory myopathy in 5
au responded to immune modifying treatment), and a non-inflammatoryle in 2 patients (Pompe disease and myotonic muscular dystrophy).
excluded a myopathic process in 3 patients found to have alternative
neurogenic pathology. CONCLUSIONS/RELEVANCE: The histopatho-
logical data from percutaneous needle muscle biopsy can be used to differ-
entiate the diagnosis of IBM from alternative neuromuscular diagnoses.

P05.114
Sensitivity of Motor Unit Potential Analysis in
Facioscapulohumeral Muscular Dystrophy Simon
Podnar, Janez Zidar, Ljubljana, Slovenia
OBJECTIVE: To assess the sensitivity of template operated motor unit
potential (MUP) analysis in patients with a molecular genetic diagnosis of
facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD). BACKGROUND: Tradi-
tionaly quantitative electromyography (EMG) was a slow and cumbersome
technique, which changed dramatically by introduction of template-
operated MUP analysis. Using this technique quantitative EMG became
feasible even in busy laboratories. However, very little information is avail-

able on sensitivity and specificity of such analyses. DESIGN/METHODS;
All registered patients with a clinical diagnosis of FSHD in Slovenia were
invited to participate. Only patients with positive genetic testing were
included. The study was approved by the National Ethics Committee of
Slovenia, and subjects provided informed consent. The strength of elbow
flexion and knee extension were assessed using the MRC scale. Quantita-
tive EMG of the right biceps brachii and vastus lateralis muscles was
performed using a standard concentric EMG needle, and a commercially
available EMG system. MUP parameters from patients’ muscles were com-
pared to reference limits for mean values, and “outliers”. Changes were
designated “myopathic” if MUP parameter values (except number of phases
and number of turns) were below the normative range. RESULTS: Quan-
titative EMG was performed in 31 patients (17 men), aged 22 to 77 years
(median, 43 years). Strength of elbow flexion/knee extension was normal in
45%/52% of patients. In each muscle, only 3 MUP parameters were needed
to obtain the same sensitivity as all 8 parameters (i.e., biceps brachii:
thickness (69%), duration (+ 14%), and amplitude (+ 7%) = 90%; vastus
lateralis: thickness (50%), area (+ 7%), and amplitude (+ 3%) = 60%).
Myopathic abnormalities were demonstrated in all weak biceps brachii
muscles, and in 77% of biceps brachii muscles with normal strength. CON-
CLUSIONS/RELEVANCE: The study demonstrated a high sensitivity of
multi-MUP analysis in FSHD.
Supported by: The Republic of Slovenia Research Agency, Grant No. J3
7899.
Disclosure: Dr. Podnar has nothing to disclose. Dr. Zidar has nothing to disclose.
PO5.115
A Videography Documented Case Report:
Antibody-Negative Stiff-Person Syndrome Joanna S.
Fong, Derk Krieger, Cleveland, OH
OBJECTIVE: Our aim is to further characterize antibody-negative Stiff-
Person Syndrome and to demonstrate its responsiveness to plasmapheresis.
BACKGROUND: Stiff-Person Syndrome (SPS) is a rare neurologic disor-
der of which only 150 cases have been reported in the past twenty-five
years. It is well recognized as an autoimmune disease directed against
synaptic antigens which causes progressive rigidity and muscle spasms.
Multiple antigens have been identified, including the GABA-synthesizing
enzyme glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), and others such as amphiphy-
sin and gephyrin. DESIGN/METHODS: We report the case of a 37 year-
old Caucasian man with a history of rheumatoid arthritis under treatment
with anti-tumor necrosis factor agents, who presented with a six-year his-
tory of progressive muscle spasms and rigidity. RESULTS: Clinical presen-
tation was most consistent with SPS, however, laboratory testing for anti-
GAD, anti-amphiphysin, CRMP-5 western blot, and VGKC antibody tests
were negative. The patient displayed a dramatic clinical response to plas-
mapheresis (5 treatments over 2 weeks), which was documented by videog-
raphy. CONCLUSIONS/RELEVANCE: This strongly suggests that SPS
is an antibody-mediated disease for which all pathogenetic antibodies are
yet to be described. Although ancillary tests such as antibody testing and
EMG are useful, the diagnosis can largely be made based on clinical pre-
sentation and response to therapy.
Disclosure: Dr. Fong has nothing to disclose. Dr. Krieger has nothing to disclose.

P05.116
ALS-Associated Cu/Zn SOD Mutant Protein Is
Linked to VEGF mRNA Destabilization and Down-

Regulation In Vitro Liang Lu, Birmingham, AL, Alvaro
Estevez, New York, Lisa Zheng, Birmingham, Shin Oh, Birming-
ham, AL, Peter King, Birmingham
OBJECTIVE: To analyze the effect of mutant copper/zinc superoxide dis-
mutase (SOD)-1 protein expression on vascular endothelial growth factor
(VEGF) RNA stability and expression. BACKGROUND: VEGF, a neuro-
protective factor, is a potent modifier of ALS phenotype in mice expressing
the SOD1 mutation. Deficiency of VEGF leads to rapid progression of motor
neuron degeneration, whereas administration of VEGF retards the disease.
